questions.title: Pro-opiomelanocortin is the precursor of ACTH
questions.question: Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) is the precursor of:

explanations.A: Correct. Pro-opiomelanocortin is a large precursor peptide made by the corticotrophs of the anterior pituitary. Post-translational cleavage of POMC yields ACTH together with melanocyte-stimulating hormone, beta-lipotropin and beta-endorphin, so ACTH is the pituitary hormone derived from POMC.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cortisol is a steroid synthesised from cholesterol by the adrenal zona fasciculata under the drive of ACTH; it is not a peptide and is not cleaved from POMC.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Growth hormone is a single-chain polypeptide transcribed from its own gene in the somatotrophs; it is not part of the POMC family.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prolactin is a distinct single-chain polypeptide made by the mammotrophs and is unrelated to POMC.
explanations.E: Incorrect. TSH is a glycoprotein of an alpha and a beta subunit encoded by separate genes; it is not derived from POMC.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ACTH (with MSH, beta-lipotropin and beta-endorphin) as the cleavage products of pro-opiomelanocortin.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.2 Pituitary p.6

questions.title: Growth hormone signals through the JAK-STAT pathway
questions.question: JAK-STAT pathways mediate the effects of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thyroid hormones are lipophilic and act on nuclear thyroid-hormone receptors that bind DNA response elements; they do not use a membrane JAK-STAT cascade.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vasopressin acts through G-protein-coupled receptors: V2 receptors raise cyclic AMP and V1 receptors raise intracellular calcium via phospholipase C, not JAK-STAT.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucagon works through a Gs-coupled receptor that raises cyclic AMP; it does not signal through JAK-STAT.
explanations.D: Correct. The growth-hormone receptor is a single-pass cytokine-family receptor with no intrinsic kinase activity. Hormone binding dimerises the receptor and activates associated JAK2 (Janus kinase 2), which phosphorylates STAT proteins; the STATs then translocate to the nucleus to alter transcription, so the JAK-STAT pathway mediates growth-hormone action.

questions.learning_objective: State that growth hormone acts through a JAK2-STAT signalling cascade.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q14 = d; Q36 = b 'activates JAK2' corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.2 Pituitary p.7 and p.10

questions.title: Growth hormone promotes protein synthesis via amino-acid transport
questions.question: Growth hormone effects include:

options.A: Growth by a direct action on the epiphyseal cartilage
options.B: Protein synthesis by increasing amino acid transport through cell membranes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Growth hormone acts on the epiphyseal cartilage mainly indirectly, by inducing hepatic somatomedins (IGF-1) which drive chondrocyte proliferation; the epiphyseal effect is not a direct GH action.
explanations.B: Correct. Growth hormone is anabolic for protein. It increases the active transport of amino acids into cells and stimulates their incorporation into protein while reducing protein catabolism. The net result is a positive nitrogen balance, which supports tissue growth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Growth hormone is diabetogenic - it decreases cellular glucose utilisation and antagonises insulin, so it does not increase glucose uptake by cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Growth hormone is lipolytic, mobilising fatty acids from adipose tissue for energy; it promotes lipolysis, not lipogenesis.

questions.learning_objective: Describe growth hormone's protein-anabolic action through increased amino-acid transport into cells.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.2 Pituitary p.6

questions.title: Somatomedins circulate bound to carrier proteins with slow release
questions.question: Somatomedins:

options.A: Are secreted from the liver to stimulate growth hormone secretion
options.B: Are insulin-like growth factors secreted by the hypothalamus
options.C: Attach strongly to carrier proteins in the blood and are released slowly to tissues
options.D: Decrease the synthesis of collagen and chondroitin sulphate

explanations.A: Incorrect. Somatomedins do feed back on growth-hormone secretion, but they inhibit it (by stimulating hypothalamic somatostatin and acting on the pituitary), rather than stimulate it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Somatomedins (insulin-like growth factors) are produced mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone, not by the hypothalamus.
explanations.C: Correct. Circulating somatomedins are almost entirely bound to specific IGF-binding proteins. This binding gives them a long plasma half-life and releases the active factor slowly to the tissues, so their action is sustained rather than pulsatile.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Somatomedins stimulate the synthesis of collagen and chondroitin sulphate by chondrocytes, promoting cartilage and bone growth; they do not decrease it.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that somatomedins circulate bound to carrier proteins, giving a long half-life and slow tissue release.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.2 Pituitary p.10

questions.title: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 water channels in the renal tubule
questions.question: The functions of ADH include:

options.A: V1 receptor activation to induce the production of prostaglandin E2
options.C: Insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the distal renal tubules
options.D: V2 receptor stimulation in pituitary corticotropes during stress

explanations.A: Incorrect. V1 receptors act through phospholipase C to cause vascular smooth-muscle contraction; renal prostaglandin E2 actually opposes ADH, so PGE2 production is not an ADH effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ADH regulates water rather than potassium handling; it does not reduce urinary potassium excretion (that is a feature of aldosterone-driven sodium-potassium exchange).
explanations.C: Correct. ADH binds V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting-duct principal cells, raising intracellular cyclic AMP. The cyclic AMP signal drives insertion of preformed aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane. Water is then reabsorbed down the medullary osmotic gradient, so a concentrated urine is formed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The renal antidiuretic action is mediated by V2 receptors on the collecting duct, not on pituitary corticotropes; ADH does potentiate ACTH release, but through V1b (V3) receptors, not V2.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the V2-receptor / cyclic-AMP / aquaporin-2 mechanism of the antidiuretic action of ADH.

questions.title: Cervical dilation stimulates oxytocin release (Ferguson reflex)
questions.question: Secretion of oxytocin is increased by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Milk ejection is the result of oxytocin action on breast myoepithelial cells, not a stimulus for its secretion; the stimulus is suckling.
explanations.B: Correct. Stretch of the cervix and vagina during labour sends afferent signals to the hypothalamus that trigger oxytocin release. The released oxytocin strengthens uterine contraction, which dilates the cervix further and evokes still more oxytocin. This self-reinforcing loop is the positive-feedback Ferguson reflex of parturition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prolactin and oxytocin are secreted in parallel during lactation, but a rise in prolactin is not itself a stimulus for oxytocin release.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A rise in extracellular fluid volume suppresses ADH, and volume is not a physiological stimulus for oxytocin secretion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cervical/vaginal stretch as the stimulus for oxytocin release in the Ferguson positive-feedback reflex.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q28 = b; Q26 = d 'cervical dilation' corroborates)

questions.title: Iodide trapping is secondary active transport
questions.question: Iodine is concentrated in thyroid follicular epithelial cells by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The iodide pump does not hydrolyse ATP directly, so it is not primary active transport; its energy comes indirectly from the sodium gradient.
explanations.B: Correct. Iodide enters the follicular cell on the basolateral sodium-iodide symporter (NIS). This carrier moves iodide against its electrochemical gradient using the inward sodium gradient maintained by the Na-K ATPase, which is the definition of secondary active transport. This iodide-trapping step concentrates iodide many-fold inside the gland.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simple diffusion moves a solute down its gradient, so it cannot concentrate iodide against its electrochemical gradient.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion is also passive and cannot accumulate iodide against its gradient.

questions.learning_objective: Classify thyroid iodide trapping by the sodium-iodide symporter as secondary active transport.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.3 Thyroid p.13

questions.title: Peripheral T4 to T3 conversion by type 1 deiodinase
questions.question: Most of the T3 in the liver is formed from circulating T4 by the action of:

explanations.A: Correct. In the liver, T3 is produced mainly by outer-ring (5'-) deiodination of T4 by type 1 deiodinase (D1). D1 is abundant in liver, kidney and thyroid and supplies most of the circulating T3. Because roughly four-fifths of plasma T3 comes from this peripheral conversion, T4 behaves largely as a prohormone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Type 2 deiodinase (D2) also generates T3 but acts intracellularly in tissues such as brain, pituitary and brown fat for local supply, not the bulk of plasma/hepatic T3.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Type 3 deiodinase (D3) is an inner-ring deiodinase that inactivates T4 and T3 to reverse T3 and T2; it does not form active T3.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no type 4 deiodinase; only three deiodinase isoenzymes (D1, D2 and D3) exist.

questions.learning_objective: Identify type 1 deiodinase as the enzyme generating most circulating T3 from peripheral T4.

questions.title: Thyroxine is transported mainly on thyroxine-binding globulin
questions.question: Most of the circulating T4 is bound to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transthyretin (prealbumin) carries only a minor fraction of circulating thyroxine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Albumin binds some thyroxine but with low affinity, so it is not the principal carrier.
explanations.C: Correct. About 70% of circulating thyroxine is carried by thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), a high-affinity plasma glycoprotein. This bound pool is a large reservoir that buffers the free-hormone concentration, with prealbumin and albumin carrying smaller fractions. Only the tiny unbound fraction is immediately available to the tissues.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thyroxine is almost entirely protein-bound and a specific carrier does exist, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that thyroxine-binding globulin carries the largest fraction of circulating T4.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.3 Thyroid p.14

questions.title: Only free (unbound) thyroxine is physiologically active
questions.question: Physiologically active thyroxine exists in which form?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thyroxine bound to albumin is part of the transport reservoir and is biologically inert until released.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thyroxine bound to prealbumin (transthyretin) is likewise a carried, inactive fraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thyroxine bound to thyroxine-binding globulin is the largest reservoir but is inactive while it remains bound.
explanations.D: Correct. Only the small unbound (free) fraction of thyroxine can cross cell membranes and reach the nuclear receptor, so the free hormone is the biologically active form. Protein-bound hormone is inert until it dissociates. This free-hormone principle is why free T4, not total T4, best reflects thyroid status.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that only the free (unbound) fraction of thyroxine is physiologically active.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.3 Thyroid p.14

questions.title: Thyroid hormone acts on nuclear receptors to change transcription
questions.question: Thyroxine hormone:

options.A: Binds a membrane receptor and activates protein synthesis
options.B: Binds a membrane receptor and activates a second messenger
options.C: Binds a nuclear receptor to affect gene transcription
options.D: Has a direct effect on the hypothalamic nuclei affecting metabolism

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thyroid hormone does not act through a membrane receptor; its principal actions are genomic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thyroid hormone does not use a membrane second-messenger cascade for its major effects.
explanations.C: Correct. Being lipophilic, thyroid hormone (chiefly T3) enters the cell and binds nuclear thyroid-hormone receptors sitting on thyroid-response elements of DNA. The hormone-receptor complex alters gene transcription, changing the synthesis of enzymes and structural proteins. This genomic mechanism accounts for the slow onset and long duration of thyroid-hormone action.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thyroid hormone acts broadly on target-tissue nuclei, not by a direct metabolic action confined to hypothalamic nuclei.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the nuclear-receptor genomic mechanism of thyroid hormone action.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q15 = c; Q28 = b corroborates nuclear action)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.3 Thyroid p.14 and p.16

questions.title: Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase (organification and coupling)
questions.question: The coupling of monoiodotyrosine and diiodotyrosine and the iodination of thyroglobulin is blocked by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. TSH stimulates every synthetic step, including iodination and coupling; it does not block them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. TRH drives TSH release and therefore promotes hormone synthesis rather than inhibiting it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Iodine is the substrate for iodination; although a very high iodide load can transiently inhibit organification (Wolff-Chaikoff effect), iodine is not the blocker meant here.
explanations.D: Correct. Thiocarbamide (thionamide) drugs such as propylthiouracil and carbimazole inhibit thyroid peroxidase, the enzyme that iodinates thyroglobulin tyrosyls and couples MIT and DIT. Blocking peroxidase halts formation of new T3 and T4. These agents are therefore used to treat hyperthyroidism.

questions.learning_objective: Identify thionamides as thyroid-peroxidase inhibitors that block iodination and coupling.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.3 Thyroid p.14

questions.title: The thyroid secretes predominantly thyroxine (T4)
questions.question: Almost all of the active thyroid hormone entering the circulation is in the form of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Only a small fraction of the hormone the gland secretes is T3; most circulating T3 is made later by peripheral deiodination of T4.
explanations.B: Correct. The thyroid secretes far more thyroxine (T4) than triiodothyronine, so almost all hormone leaving the gland is T4. T4 then acts as a circulating prohormone that is deiodinated to the more active T3 in the tissues. This is why T4 is the predominant thyroid hormone measured in plasma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thyroglobulin is the intrafollicular storage protein and is not normally released into the blood in significant amounts.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thyrotropin (TSH) is an anterior-pituitary hormone, not a thyroid secretory product.
explanations.E: Incorrect. LATS is a thyroid-stimulating autoantibody found in Graves disease, not a normal thyroid secretion.

questions.learning_objective: State that thyroxine (T4) is the predominant hormone secreted by the thyroid gland.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q8 = b; Q10 = a corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.3 Thyroid p.13

questions.title: Thyroid hormone is stored in colloid as thyroglobulin
questions.question: Iodides are stored in the thyroid follicles mainly in the form of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thyroxine is present as residues within thyroglobulin, but it is not stored as free hormone; it is released only after proteolysis.
explanations.B: Correct. Iodinated tyrosyl residues are stored as part of the large glycoprotein thyroglobulin in the colloid of the follicle. This lets the thyroid hold several weeks' supply of hormone extracellularly, a feature unique among endocrine glands. Hormone is released when follicular cells endocytose colloid and lysosomal proteases split T3 and T4 from thyroglobulin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Monoiodotyrosine is an iodinated intermediate residue on thyroglobulin, not the storage macromolecule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Diiodotyrosine is likewise an iodinated residue coupled within thyroglobulin rather than the storage form itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that thyroid hormone is stored in follicular colloid bound within thyroglobulin.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.3 Thyroid p.12

questions.title: PTH stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to activate vitamin D
questions.question: Which of the following is a direct effect of parathyroid hormone (PTH)?

options.C: Increased intestinal synthesis of calcium-binding protein

explanations.A: Incorrect. PTH does raise osteoclastic resorption, but indirectly through osteoblast RANKL; osteoclasts lack PTH receptors, so this is not a direct PTH effect.
explanations.B: Correct. PTH acts directly on the renal proximal tubule to stimulate 1-alpha-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). The resulting calcitriol then raises intestinal calcium absorption. Thus PTH's intestinal effect is indirect, mediated by activation of vitamin D.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intestinal calcium-binding protein (calbindin) is induced by calcitriol, not directly by PTH.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PTH inhibits proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption (causing phosphaturia); it does not increase it.

questions.learning_objective: State that PTH stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, activating vitamin D to raise calcium.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q1 = b; Q27 = d 'final activation of vitamin D' corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.19 and p.23

questions.title: Calcitonin lowers plasma calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts
questions.question: Which of the following hormones lowers the plasma level of ionized calcium?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Calcineurin is an intracellular phosphatase in signal transduction, not a calcium-regulating hormone.
explanations.B: Correct. Calcitonin, secreted by thyroid parafollicular C cells when plasma calcium rises, lowers ionized calcium mainly by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption. It also increases urinary calcium excretion. Its actions therefore oppose those of PTH.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Parathyroid hormone raises, rather than lowers, plasma calcium.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PTH-related peptide mimics PTH and raises calcium, as in humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy.

questions.learning_objective: State that calcitonin lowers plasma calcium chiefly by inhibiting osteoclasts.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q13 = b; Q15 = b, Q20 = d, Q24 = b corroborate)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.21-22

questions.title: PTH acts on osteoblast receptors to drive osteoclasts (RANKL)
questions.question: Parathyroid hormone:

options.A: Increases intestinal absorption of Ca2+ independent of 1,25(OH)2 D3
options.B: Binds osteoblastic receptors to stimulate osteoclast activity
options.C: Secretion is increased by a rise in plasma Ca2+ concentration

explanations.A: Incorrect. PTH increases intestinal calcium absorption indirectly through 1,25(OH)2 D3, not independently of it.
explanations.B: Correct. Osteoclasts have no PTH receptors; PTH binds receptors on osteoblasts and stromal cells, which then express RANKL. RANKL engages RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their maturation and bone resorption, releasing calcium. So PTH stimulates osteoclasts only indirectly, via osteoblasts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. PTH secretion is stimulated by a fall, not a rise, in plasma ionized calcium.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PTH increases the production of 1,25(OH)2 D3 by stimulating renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that PTH acts on osteoblast receptors (RANKL) to stimulate osteoclastic resorption.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.21-22

questions.title: PTH stimulates distal-tubule calcium reabsorption
questions.question: Which of the following results from the action of parathyroid hormone on the renal tubule?

options.B: Stimulation of Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal tubule
options.C: Stimulation of phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
options.D: Interaction with receptors on the luminal membrane of proximal tubular cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. PTH stimulates, rather than inhibits, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
explanations.B: Correct. PTH acts on the distal convoluted tubule to increase active calcium reabsorption, reducing urinary calcium loss and helping to raise plasma calcium. This renal action complements its effects on bone and on vitamin D. At the same time PTH inhibits proximal phosphate reabsorption, producing phosphaturia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. PTH inhibits proximal phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia); it does not stimulate it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PTH binds receptors on the basolateral (peritubular) membrane, not the luminal membrane, of tubular cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that PTH increases distal-tubule calcium reabsorption while causing proximal phosphaturia.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.21

questions.title: The PTH receptor is a cell-membrane (GPCR) receptor
questions.question: The receptor for parathyroid hormone is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cytoplasmic receptors serve lipophilic hormones; PTH is a peptide and cannot cross the membrane to reach one.
explanations.B: Correct. PTH is a peptide hormone that binds a G-protein-coupled receptor on the target-cell membrane. Receptor activation raises intracellular cyclic AMP (and IP3/calcium), which mediates PTH's renal and bone actions. Being water-soluble, PTH cannot enter the cell to reach an intracellular receptor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nuclear receptors bind lipophilic hormones such as steroids and thyroid hormone, not peptide PTH.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The PTH receptor is a specific membrane GPCR, not a non-specific binding site.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the PTH receptor as a membrane G-protein-coupled receptor acting via cyclic AMP.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.23

questions.title: The first-line calcium buffer is exchange with the labile bone pool
questions.question: The first line of defence to buffer rapid changes of plasma calcium is:

options.A: Rapid shift of calcium from the labile calcium pool to or from plasma

explanations.A: Correct. The fastest buffer of plasma calcium is the hormone-independent physicochemical exchange between plasma and a readily exchangeable ('labile') pool of calcium in bone and other tissues. This exchange acts within minutes, before hormonal responses can develop. PTH and vitamin D then provide slower, sustained correction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. PTH secretion is a hormonal response that takes longer than the immediate physicochemical exchange.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Activation of vitamin D and its intestinal effect develop over hours to days, not immediately.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A change in calcitonin is a minor and slower influence, not the first-line rapid buffer.

questions.learning_objective: Identify rapid exchange with the labile bone calcium pool as the first-line plasma-calcium buffer.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.22

questions.title: Vitamin D is synthesised in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol
questions.question: All the following about vitamin D are correct, EXCEPT:

options.B: It is essential for normal calcification of bone in childhood
options.C: It requires hepatic modification for activation
options.D: It cannot be synthesized in the body

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true statement). Vitamin D deficiency lowers calcium and drives a secondary rise in PTH, so this statement is correct and is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true statement). Vitamin D is required for normal bone mineralisation, and its deficiency causes rickets in children, so this is correct.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true statement). Vitamin D is 25-hydroxylated in the liver (then 1-alpha-hydroxylated in the kidney), so hepatic modification is genuinely required.
explanations.D: Correct (the false statement, hence the exception). Vitamin D can be made in the body: ultraviolet light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3). The claim that it cannot be synthesised is therefore wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that vitamin D3 is synthesised in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol under UV light.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.21

questions.title: Low calcium with high PTH indicates vitamin D deficiency
questions.question: A decrease in plasma ionized calcium together with an increase in PTH is most likely found in a patient with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. In hypoparathyroidism PTH is low, not raised, so it cannot explain a high PTH.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary hyperparathyroidism raises PTH, but the plasma calcium is high, not low.
explanations.C: Correct. Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium absorption and lowers plasma ionized calcium. The low calcium then drives a compensatory (secondary) rise in PTH. The combination of low ionized calcium with high PTH is therefore typical of vitamin D deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin D excess raises calcium absorption and plasma calcium, which suppresses PTH.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise low ionized calcium with high PTH as secondary hyperparathyroidism of vitamin D deficiency.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.4 Calcium p.20

questions.title: Cortisol is anti-inflammatory by reducing prostaglandin formation
questions.question: The anti-inflammatory effect of cortisol is thought to be due to:

options.C: Increased release of proteolytic enzymes from lysosomes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cortisol reduces, not increases, leukotriene formation by limiting arachidonic-acid release.
explanations.B: Correct. Cortisol induces lipocortin (annexin-1), which inhibits phospholipase A2 and so reduces the liberation of arachidonic acid. With less arachidonic acid, the formation of prostaglandins (and leukotrienes) falls, producing the anti-inflammatory effect. Cortisol also stabilises lysosomal membranes and suppresses inflammatory cytokines.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cortisol stabilises lysosomal membranes and decreases release of proteolytic enzymes, the opposite of this option.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cortisol inhibits phospholipase A2 (through lipocortin); it does not activate it.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that cortisol is anti-inflammatory by inhibiting phospholipase A2 and reducing prostaglandins.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q6 = b; Q25 = d corroborates the anti-inflammatory profile)

questions.title: Aldosterone is regulated mainly by potassium and angiotensin II, not ACTH
questions.question: Aldosterone secretion is markedly increased by an increase in plasma:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A rise in plasma volume suppresses aldosterone by reducing renin and angiotensin II, rather than increasing it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A rise in plasma sodium tends to lower aldosterone; it is hyponatraemia, not hypernatraemia, that stimulates it.
explanations.C: Correct. The two principal stimuli to aldosterone are angiotensin II and a rise in plasma potassium, and even a small increase in plasma K+ directly stimulates the zona glomerulosa. ACTH is only a minor, permissive regulator. Hence hyperkalaemia markedly increases aldosterone secretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ACTH exerts only a small permissive effect and is the least important regulator of aldosterone.

questions.learning_objective: State that aldosterone is controlled mainly by angiotensin II and plasma potassium, with ACTH minor.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q8 = c; Q14 = a 'ACTH least important' corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.5 Adrenal p.25-26

questions.title: The zona glomerulosa is the sole source of aldosterone
questions.question: Selective destruction of the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex would produce a deficiency of:

explanations.A: Correct. The zona glomerulosa, the outermost cortical zone, is the only site that expresses aldosterone synthase, so it is the exclusive source of the mineralocorticoid aldosterone. Its selective destruction therefore causes aldosterone deficiency. The other cortical zones are spared.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Androstenedione is an androgen produced by the zona reticularis, not the glomerulosa.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cortisol is made in the zona fasciculata, so loss of the glomerulosa does not cause cortisol deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dehydroepiandrosterone is an androgen of the zona reticularis and is unaffected by glomerulosa destruction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the zona glomerulosa as the exclusive source of aldosterone.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.5 Adrenal p.25-26

questions.title: Adrenal androgen secretion is driven by ACTH
questions.question: Release of androgens from the adrenal cortex is stimulated mainly by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. LH stimulates gonadal steroid production in the testis and ovary, not adrenal androgen secretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. FSH acts on gonadal cells such as Sertoli and granulosa cells, not on the adrenal cortex.
explanations.C: Correct. Adrenal androgens, mainly DHEA and androstenedione, are produced by the zona reticularis, whose secretion is driven by ACTH, the same trophic hormone that controls cortisol. This is why ACTH excess raises adrenal androgens, as in congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Gonadotrophins do not control the adrenal cortex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. GnRH acts on the pituitary to release gonadotrophins and has no direct action on adrenal androgen output.

questions.learning_objective: State that ACTH is the main stimulus for adrenal androgen (zona reticularis) secretion.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.5 Adrenal p.26

questions.title: Glucocorticoids reduce circulating lymphocytes
questions.question: Glucocorticoids decrease the number of circulating:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucocorticoids increase circulating neutrophils by demargination, rather than decreasing them.
explanations.B: Correct. Glucocorticoids reduce circulating lymphocytes and eosinophils by redistribution out of the blood and by apoptosis. At the same time they raise neutrophils, so the characteristic blood picture is lymphopenia and eosinopenia with neutrophilia. This contributes to their immunosuppressive effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Platelet counts are not characteristically lowered by glucocorticoids.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucocorticoids tend to raise the red-cell count slightly, not lower it.

questions.learning_objective: State that glucocorticoids cause lymphopenia and eosinopenia with neutrophilia.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.5 Adrenal p.26

questions.title: Chronically high ACTH causes hyperpigmentation
questions.question: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH):

options.A: Is an important physiologic regulator of aldosterone secretion
options.B: Is secreted at a constant level throughout the day
options.C: Causes hyperpigmentation whenever it is chronically increased
options.D: Has no effect on the size of cells in the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis

explanations.A: Incorrect. ACTH is only a minor regulator of aldosterone; angiotensin II and potassium are the main controllers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ACTH is secreted with a circadian rhythm that peaks in the early morning, not at a constant level.
explanations.C: Correct. ACTH is cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin and shares its N-terminal sequence with melanocyte-stimulating hormone, so chronically raised ACTH stimulates melanocytes and produces skin hyperpigmentation. This is seen in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) and in ectopic-ACTH syndromes. It is a useful clinical marker of a high-ACTH state.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ACTH is trophic for the zona fasciculata and reticularis; chronic excess enlarges these cells, and its loss causes cortical atrophy.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that chronically high ACTH causes hyperpigmentation through its MSH-like activity.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q22 = c; Q2 = d Addison hyperpigmentation corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.5 Adrenal p.24 and p.27

questions.title: Atrial natriuretic peptide increases renal sodium excretion
questions.question: Which of the following hormones increases sodium excretion in the kidney?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and conserves sodium, rather than promoting its excretion.
explanations.B: Correct. Atrial natriuretic peptide is released from atrial myocytes when they are stretched by a rise in blood volume. It increases renal sodium and water excretion by raising GFR and inhibiting tubular sodium reabsorption, and it suppresses renin and aldosterone. The net effect lowers blood volume and pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cortisol has weak mineralocorticoid activity and tends to promote sodium retention, not excretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angiotensin II promotes sodium reabsorption and stimulates aldosterone, reducing sodium excretion.

questions.learning_objective: State that atrial natriuretic peptide promotes renal sodium excretion and opposes aldosterone.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.5 Adrenal p.27

questions.title: Cushing syndrome features truncal obesity
questions.question: Cushing syndrome is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cushing syndrome is caused by glucocorticoid (cortisol) excess, not by hypersecretion of aldosterone.
explanations.B: Correct. Cortisol excess causes central redistribution of fat, giving truncal (central) obesity with a moon face and buffalo hump, together with purple abdominal striae, muscle wasting and hyperglycaemia. These are the classic features of Cushing syndrome. The catabolic action on protein also thins the skin and weakens muscle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ACTH may be high (ACTH-dependent pituitary or ectopic causes) or low (adrenal or exogenous causes), so it is not always low.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cortisol excess causes lymphopenia, not lymphocytosis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise truncal obesity and striae as classic features of cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q30 = b; Q11 = b striae, Q23 = c moon face corroborate)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.5 Adrenal p.25-28

questions.title: Insulin-dependent glucose uptake uses GLUT4
questions.question: Insulin-dependent glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue is mainly mediated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. GLUT1 mediates basal, insulin-independent glucose uptake in cells such as red cells and the blood-brain barrier.
explanations.B: Incorrect. GLUT2 is a high-capacity transporter of the liver and pancreatic beta cells, not the insulin-responsive muscle/fat transporter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GLUT3 is a high-affinity neuronal transporter and is insulin-independent.
explanations.D: Correct. Insulin stimulates glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue by recruiting GLUT4 transporters from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane. When insulin falls, GLUT4 is internalised, so uptake in these tissues is insulin-dependent. This is why muscle and fat glucose uptake drops in insulin deficiency.

questions.learning_objective: State that insulin-dependent glucose uptake in muscle and fat is mediated by GLUT4 recruitment.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.31

questions.title: Beta-cell glucose sensing uses GLUT2
questions.question: Insulin secretion from beta cells of the pancreas in response to a glucose load is mediated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. GLUT1 provides basal uptake in other tissues but is not the beta-cell glucose sensor.
explanations.B: Correct. Pancreatic beta cells take up glucose through GLUT2, a high-Km transporter whose uptake rate tracks the blood glucose level. Glucose is phosphorylated by glucokinase and metabolised, raising ATP, which closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarises the cell and triggers insulin release. GLUT2 therefore couples plasma glucose to insulin secretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GLUT3 is a neuronal transporter, not the beta-cell sensor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of muscle and fat, not the beta-cell glucose sensor.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pancreatic beta cell senses glucose through the GLUT2 transporter.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.31

questions.title: Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
questions.question: Glucagon hormone (indicate the one correct characteristic):

options.A: It is secreted by pancreatic D-cells
options.B: Its secretion is stimulated by an increase in blood glucose
options.D: It produces its action by binding to a cytoplasmic receptor

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucagon is secreted by the alpha cells of the islets, not the delta (D) cells, which make somatostatin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucagon secretion is stimulated by a fall, not a rise, in blood glucose.
explanations.C: Correct. Glucagon is the main hyperglycaemic hormone: acting on the liver it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, raising hepatic glucose output and blood glucose. It also promotes lipolysis and ketogenesis during fasting. Its actions oppose those of insulin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucagon is a peptide that binds a membrane G-protein-coupled receptor and acts through cyclic AMP, not a cytoplasmic receptor.

questions.learning_objective: State that glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q4 = c; Q3 = c, Q29 = c corroborate)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.29 and p.33

questions.title: Glucagon secretion is stimulated by hypoglycaemia
questions.question: Glucagon secretion is induced by:

options.B: Low serum concentration of amino acids
options.D: Secretion of somatostatin by pancreatic delta cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperglycaemia suppresses glucagon secretion rather than stimulating it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A rise in amino acids, not a fall, stimulates glucagon; low amino acids do not induce it.
explanations.C: Correct. The principal stimulus for glucagon secretion is hypoglycaemia: a fall in blood glucose triggers alpha-cell glucagon release, which restores glucose by hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. This mirrors insulin, which is released when glucose is high. Amino acids and sympathetic activity also stimulate glucagon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Somatostatin from delta cells inhibits glucagon secretion; it does not induce it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hypoglycaemia as the principal stimulus for glucagon secretion.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q6 = c; Q27 = c corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.29 and p.33

questions.title: Alpha-adrenergic activation inhibits insulin secretion
questions.question: Insulin secretion from beta-cells in the pancreas is inhibited by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholine (parasympathetic) stimulates insulin secretion rather than inhibiting it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beta-adrenergic activation stimulates insulin release; it is the alpha effect that inhibits.
explanations.C: Correct. Sympathetic activity acting on alpha-2 adrenergic receptors of the beta cell inhibits insulin secretion, which is appropriate in stress or exercise when glucose must be spared. This alpha effect dominates the sympathetic response. Acetylcholine and beta-adrenergic activity, in contrast, promote insulin release.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucagon actually stimulates insulin secretion by a paracrine effect, rather than inhibiting it.

questions.learning_objective: State that alpha-adrenergic (sympathetic) activation inhibits insulin secretion.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.31

questions.title: Insulin increases Na+-K+ ATPase activity, driving potassium into cells
questions.question: Insulin hormone:

options.A: Inhibits the use of ketoacids by peripheral tissue
options.B: Transports glucose freely into liver cells through an insulin-sensitive GLUT2
options.C: Stimulates glucose reabsorption in the kidney
options.D: Increases activity of the Na+-K+ ATPase in cell membranes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Insulin promotes rather than inhibits substrate use and is antiketogenic, so this statement is wrong.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hepatic glucose uptake is via GLUT2 but is not insulin-dependent; GLUT2 is not an insulin-sensitive transporter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Insulin does not stimulate renal glucose reabsorption, which is handled by SGLT/GLUT independent of insulin.
explanations.D: Correct. Insulin increases the activity of the Na+-K+ ATPase in cell membranes, driving potassium into cells together with glucose. This is why insulin lowers plasma potassium and is used to treat hyperkalaemia. It supports the anabolic, gradient-dependent transport that insulin promotes.

questions.learning_objective: State that insulin stimulates the Na+-K+ ATPase, driving potassium into cells.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.32

questions.title: Islet cell types: F cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide, not gastrin
questions.question: Which of the following is incorrectly paired?

explanations.A: Incorrect (correctly paired). Beta cells secrete insulin, so this pairing is right and is not the wrong one.
explanations.B: Correct (the incorrect pairing). The F cells (PP cells) of the islets secrete pancreatic polypeptide, not gastrin. Gastrin is produced by the G cells of the gastric antrum and duodenum, not by the pancreatic islets. Pairing F cells with gastrin is therefore wrong, making this the answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect (correctly paired). Delta cells secrete somatostatin, a correct pairing.
explanations.D: Incorrect (correctly paired). Alpha cells secrete glucagon, a correct pairing.

questions.learning_objective: Match the islet cell types to their hormones (alpha/glucagon, beta/insulin, delta/somatostatin, F/pancreatic polypeptide).

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.30

questions.title: Adipose glucose uptake is insulin-dependent, unlike brain and red cells
questions.question: Even without insulin, glucose uptake is adequate in all the following tissues EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct (the exception). Adipose tissue depends on insulin for glucose uptake because it uses the insulin-responsive GLUT4 transporter. Without insulin, GLUT4 is internalised and adipose glucose uptake becomes inadequate. Adipose tissue is therefore the exception among these tissues.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intestinal mucosa takes up glucose independently of insulin, so its uptake is adequate without insulin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The brain takes up glucose through insulin-independent GLUT1 and GLUT3, so it does not require insulin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Red blood cells take up glucose through insulin-independent GLUT1, so their uptake is adequate without insulin.

questions.learning_objective: Contrast insulin-independent tissues (brain, red cells, gut) with insulin-dependent adipose and muscle.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.6 Pancreas p.29

questions.title: Spermatogenesis requires FSH and testosterone
questions.question: Which hormones are responsible for spermatogenesis?

explanations.A: Correct. Spermatogenesis requires both FSH, which acts on the Sertoli cells, and a high local concentration of testosterone produced by Leydig cells under LH. FSH and testosterone act together on the Sertoli cells to support the developing germ cells. Neither hormone alone is sufficient for full spermatogenesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. LH acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone and inhibin restrains FSH; this pair does not itself drive spermatogenesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GnRH acts on the pituitary and inhibin inhibits FSH, so this pair does not directly support spermatogenesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prolactin and growth hormone are not the hormones responsible for spermatogenesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that spermatogenesis requires both FSH and testosterone acting on Sertoli cells.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q4 = a; Q1 = d corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.7 Male reproduction p.34

questions.title: Dihydrotestosterone is the most potent androgen
questions.question: Which hormone is the most potent (active) form of testosterone?

explanations.A: Correct. Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is the most potent androgen: it is formed from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase in target tissues and binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity than testosterone. DHT mediates many androgenic effects, such as external genital and prostate development. It is therefore the most active form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Androstenedione is a weak androgen precursor, far less potent than DHT.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dehydroepiandrosterone is a weak adrenal androgen precursor, not the most potent form.
explanations.D: Incorrect. These androgens differ greatly in potency, so 'all of the above' is wrong; DHT is the most potent.

questions.learning_objective: Identify dihydrotestosterone as the most potent androgen, formed by 5-alpha-reductase.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.7 Male reproduction p.35

questions.title: Estrogen increases sex-hormone-binding globulin
questions.question: Which of the following increases the level of sex-hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) in plasma?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Androgens tend to lower SHBG rather than raise it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Growth hormone does not raise SHBG and tends to lower it.
explanations.C: Correct. Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of sex-hormone-binding globulin, raising plasma SHBG. This is why SHBG rises in pregnancy and with oestrogen therapy, which lowers the free fraction of circulating sex steroids. Androgens have the opposite effect on SHBG.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neither testosterone nor growth hormone raises SHBG, so this combination is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that estrogen raises hepatic synthesis of sex-hormone-binding globulin.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.7 Male reproduction p.35-36

questions.title: Seminal vesicles secrete fructose as sperm energy source
questions.question: The normal seminal ejaculate:

options.A: Has a volume of about 5-10 ml
options.B: Comes mainly from the seminiferous tubules and epididymis
options.C: Contains fructose from the seminal vesicles

explanations.A: Incorrect. Normal ejaculate volume is about 2-5 ml, not 5-10 ml.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Most of the seminal volume comes from the accessory glands (seminal vesicles and prostate), not from the tubules and epididymis.
explanations.C: Correct. The seminal vesicles secrete fructose into the semen, which is the main energy substrate for sperm motility. Seminal fructose is a marker of seminal-vesicle secretion and of patency of the ejaculatory ducts. Its absence suggests seminal-vesicle or ductal obstruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Semen is alkaline, not acidic, to buffer the acidity of the vagina.

questions.learning_objective: State that seminal-vesicle fructose is the main energy substrate for sperm.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.7 Male reproduction p.36

questions.title: cAMP is the second messenger of FSH
questions.question: Which of the following acts as a second messenger for FSH hormone?

explanations.A: Correct. FSH, like LH and TSH, is a glycoprotein hormone that binds a G-protein-coupled receptor and acts through the Gs / adenylate-cyclase pathway, raising cyclic AMP as its second messenger. Cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A to produce the response, such as aromatase induction in granulosa cells. FSH does not act through a nuclear or a principally calcium-based pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DNA is the genetic template, not a second messenger.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Calcium is the second messenger for Gq-coupled hormones, not the principal messenger for FSH.
explanations.D: Incorrect. mRNA carries transcriptional information and is not a second messenger.

questions.learning_objective: State that FSH signals through a G-protein-coupled receptor using cyclic AMP.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.8 Female reproduction p.40

questions.title: Progesterone drives the secretory transformation of the endometrium
questions.question: Which of the following hormones produces the shift in the histologic appearance of the endometrium to the secretory phase?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Estrogen drives the proliferative phase, not the secretory transformation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. FSH acts on the ovary and does not directly transform the endometrium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. LH triggers ovulation and corpus-luteum formation but does not itself produce the secretory endometrium.
explanations.D: Correct. After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which converts the estrogen-primed proliferative endometrium into the secretory phase: the glands become tortuous and secrete glycogen and the spiral arteries develop. This prepares the endometrium for implantation. Progesterone is therefore the hormone of the secretory phase.

questions.learning_objective: State that progesterone converts the proliferative endometrium into the secretory phase.

field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.8 Female reproduction p.40

questions.title: Granulosa aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol (two-cell model)
questions.question: Aromatase acting on testosterone in the granulosa cells of the ovary results in synthesis of:

explanations.A: Correct. In the two-cell model, theca cells make androgens (testosterone and androstenedione) under LH, and these diffuse to the granulosa cells where FSH-induced aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol. Estradiol is thus the main estrogen of the growing follicle. This theca-granulosa cooperation underlies follicular estrogen synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aromatase acting on testosterone yields estradiol; estrone arises mainly from aromatisation of androstenedione.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Estriol is a weak estrogen formed largely in the placenta during pregnancy, not the granulosa product here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progesterone is a corpus-luteum product; aromatase does not synthesise it.

questions.learning_objective: Describe granulosa-cell aromatisation of testosterone to estradiol in the two-cell model.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key (Q24 = a; Q22 = a granulosa estrogen corroborates)
field_notes.kasr: Dr Shebl physiology bank, Ch.8 Female reproduction p.41

questions.title: Progesterone decreases uterine contractility in pregnancy
questions.question: Progesterone:

options.A: Stimulates development of the ducts of the breast
options.D: Plasma levels remain constant after implantation

explanations.A: Incorrect. Progesterone develops the breast alveoli (lobules), whereas estrogen develops the ducts.
explanations.B: Correct. Progesterone relaxes uterine smooth muscle, decreasing myometrial contractility and excitability during pregnancy to maintain gestation (the progesterone block). A decline in progesterone activity near term contributes to the onset of labour. This quieting of the uterus is a key pregnancy-maintaining action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because option A is wrong (ducts are an estrogen effect), the combination in C cannot be correct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progesterone rises after implantation, secreted by the corpus luteum and later the placenta; it does not remain constant.

questions.learning_objective: State that progesterone reduces uterine contractility to maintain pregnancy.
